UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

DIXON, et al.,
    Plaintiffs,

v.

ALLIED MANUFACTURING, INC.,
    Defendant.

Case No. M-2024-409

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════
PARTNER-APPROVED FINAL DRAFT — FLSA OPPOSITION BRIEF
Approved by: Hassan Farooqui (Senior Partner)
Status: READY FOR FILING — USE THIS EXACT TEXT
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

PLAINTIFF'S OPPOSITION TO DEFENDANT'S MOTION TO DISMISS

I. INTRODUCTION

Plaintiffs bring this action under the Fair Labor Standards Act ("FLSA"), 29 U.S.C. § 201 et seq., seeking unpaid wages and overtime compensation on behalf of a class of workers engaged by Allied Manufacturing, Inc. ("Allied"). Allied has moved to dismiss, arguing that the workers were properly classified as independent contractors. For the reasons set forth herein, Defendant's motion should be denied.

II. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

Allied Manufacturing engaged approximately 340 workers in assembly and production roles. Allied set compensation rates, assigned work locations, controlled production methods, and maintained the right to terminate workers at will.

III. LEGAL STANDARD

To survive a motion to dismiss, a complaint must allege sufficient facts to state a claim for relief that is plausible on its face. Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007). The FLSA must be construed broadly to effectuate its remedial purposes. The economic reality test governs worker classification under the FLSA.

IV. ARGUMENT

A. Under the Economic Reality Test, the Class Members Are Employees

Courts apply the "economic reality" test to determine whether workers are employees under the FLSA. The test examines: (1) the degree of control exercised by the alleged employer; (2) the worker's opportunity for profit or loss; (3) the worker's investment in equipment or materials; (4) the permanency of the relationship; and (5) whether the service rendered is integral to the alleged employer's business.

Plaintiff acknowledges that at least a subset of the affected workers exercised significant entrepreneurial control over their work schedules and methods, satisfying key economic reality factors for independent contractor status, and that Allied Manufacturing relied in good faith on outside counsel's classification guidance. Nevertheless, the totality of the economic relationship—including Allied's control over compensation, assignment of work, and integration of workers into its core assembly operations—demonstrates employee status for the class as a whole.

B. Allied's Control Over Workers Was Pervasive

Allied Manufacturing exercised extensive control over the manner and means of the workers' performance. Allied assigned specific tasks, set production quotas, dictated work methods, and retained the right to discharge workers at will.

C. The Good Faith Defense Does Not Bar Liability

Allied contends that its classification decisions were made in good faith reliance on outside counsel. However, the good faith defense under 29 U.S.C. § 259 requires reliance on a written administrative regulation, order, ruling, approval, or interpretation of the Wage and Hour Division. Reliance on private counsel alone does not satisfy this statutory standard.

D. Plaintiffs Are Entitled to Liquidated Damages

Under the FLSA, an employer who violates the Act's overtime provisions is liable for liquidated damages equal to the amount of unpaid wages. 29 U.S.C. § 216(b).

V. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, Plaintiff respectfully requests that this Court deny Allied Manufacturing's Motion to Dismiss in its entirety.

Respectfully submitted,
[Counsel for Plaintiffs]
